summary: Proposes an extension to BGP route selection that avoids unneeded switches between external paths under certain conditions. This helps network stability and eliminates certain route oscillations. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: If two roads are about equally good, keep using the one you have instead of switching back and forth.

subtitle: Keep the current external BGP path instead of flipping on a coin-toss tie-breaker.

tldr.problem: The last BGP tie-breakers compare BGP identifiers and peering addresses, which for external peers are effectively random from the local speaker's view, so best paths can switch for no good reason and sometimes oscillate.
tldr.mechanism: If the existing best path and a new candidate are both external and neither is eliminated before the BGP identifier comparison step, keep the existing best path.
tldr.outcome: It reduces needless routing changes and removes certain route oscillations, though not the permanent oscillation cases described in RFC 3345.

facts.label: Not applied to
facts.value: Confederation peers and parallel sessions with identical BGP identifier

today: RFC 5004 is a Proposed Standard from September 2007. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Random Tie-Breaker
sections.content:
The last two steps of BGP route selection (RFC 4271, section 9.1.2.2) compare BGP identifiers and peering addresses. The identifier of a speaker is allocated by the Autonomous System it belongs to.

So for a route from an external peer, the identifier is just a random number as far as the local speaker is concerned, and the result of those steps is effectively random. This memo builds on that observation.
sections.plainLanguage: When two choices tie, BGP picks using a number that someone else chose. That is like picking a winner by a stranger's lucky number.

sections.title: The Rule
sections.content:
Suppose the existing best path A is from an external peer, and another external path B would be chosen as the new best path by the algorithm in RFC 4271. If neither A nor B is eliminated before step f), the BGP identifier comparison, the existing best path A is kept.

The algorithm SHOULD NOT be applied when either path is from a BGP Confederation peer. It also SHOULD NOT be applied when both paths come from peers with an identical BGP identifier, which means parallel BGP sessions between two speakers. Peering addresses for such sessions are typically allocated by one AS, and leaving the rule off keeps address allocation a simple tool for influencing route selection.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are already on a road and the other road is no better, stay put. There are a couple of cases, like two lanes from the same neighbor, where the old rule still applies.

sections.title: The Benefits and an Oscillation Example
sections.content:
Avoiding needless best-path transitions reduces routing and forwarding changes and helps network stability. More importantly, it can remove certain BGP route oscillations in which more than one external path from one speaker contributes to the churn.

The RFC gives an example with four routers, R1 to R4, in one AS. R1 is a route reflector with client R3, and R2 is a route reflector with client R4. Because of route reflection (RFC 4456) and the MED attribute, the best path on R1 keeps churning between (a) and (c), and on R3 between (a) and (b). With the new rule, R3 does not switch from (a) to (b) even after R1 withdraws (c), and that is enough to stop the oscillation.

Permanent oscillation scenarios described in RFC 3345 are not eliminated by this mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes two helpers keep changing their minds because of each other, and the change never stops. If each one sticks with its first choice, the changing stops.

sections.title: Deployment and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The algorithm is backward-compatible and can be deployed on a per-BGP-speaker basis. Deployment is highly recommended on a speaker with multiple external BGP peers, especially ones connecting to an inter-exchange point.

Compared with existing behavior, it may add some non-determinism to route selection. The authors argue that the identifier comparison already adds randomness, that the non-determinism has not been shown to be detrimental in practice, and that it can be removed by existing mechanisms such as setting LOCAL_PREF or MED.
sections.plainLanguage: Any one router can start doing this on its own without asking the others. It might make choices a little harder to predict, but you can still set rules to force a particular choice.

sections.title: Security and Origins
sections.content:
The RFC states that the extension does not introduce any security issues.

The acknowledgments say the idea was inspired by a route oscillation case observed in the BBN/Genuity network in 1998, and that the algorithm was also implemented and deployed at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say this change does not open any new doors for attackers. The idea came from a real problem they saw in 1998.
